label: text
content: ## Sequences

label: text
content: - Information is encoded in living cells (mostly) in the form of "sequences":

label: text
content: DNA sequences (nucleotide sequences; nucleic acids; double-stranded; ACGT)

label: text
content: RNA sequences (nucleotide sequences; nucleic acids; single-stranded; ACGU)

label: text
content: protein sequences (amino acid sequences; polypeptides; 20 "letters")

label: text
content: - This is one of the main reasons of the success of applying information science to the study of biological molecules

label: text
content: - Biological function largely depends on the 3D structure of large molecules (e.g., protein-protein interactions, DNA binding of transcription factors, etc.), but many characteristics or functions can also be inferred from the 1D structure (the sequences)

label: text
content: Gene activity (gene "expression") can be measured by sequencing RNA molecules

label: text
content: Alternative splicing can be identified by sequencing RNA molecules

label: text
content: 3D structure can (often) be predicted from the sequence (proteins, RNA molecules)

label: text
content: The genome sequence can be searched for sequence patterns to identify new genes

label: text
content: ## Alphabets and strings

label: text
content: - Let $\Sigma$ be a finite set of symbols (=characters), called the alphabet. No assumption is made about the nature of the symbols.

label: text
content: E. g., for DNA sequences, we usually consider $\Sigma = \{A,C,G,T}$ (and for RNA instead of T), but there may actually be additional symbols (e.g. $\mathrm {A},$ or $\mathrm {T}$ ... $

label: text
content: - Sequence: a set of elements ordered so that they can be labeled/enumerated with positive integers; repetitions are allowed

label: text
content: ★ In biology: usually 1-based numbering (i.e., starting from 1, not from 0)

label: text
content: - Orientation of DNA/RNA sequences: from 5' to 3' (see first lecture)

label: text
content: ★ Orientation of protein sequences: from N-terminus to C-terminus (see first lecture)

label: text
content: ★ Double-stranded DNA is usually represented by a single strand (the other strand is its "reverse complement")

label: text
content: - The length of a string S is the number of symbols in S (the length of the sequence) and can be any non-negative integer; it is often denoted as $|S|$

label: text
content: - The empty string is the unique string over $\Sigma$ of length 0, and is denoted $\varepsilon$

label: text
content: ## Protein sequences

label: text
content: - Protein sequences are usually represented by strings over a 20-letter alphabet: $ \Sigma = \{A,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,K,L,N,P,Q,R,S,T,V,W,Y}

label: text
content: - These 20 letters are usually sufficient, but:

label: text
content: The "mysterious" 21st amino acid (selenocysteine) is denoted by "U"

label: text
content: > "Unknown" amino acids in a sequence are denoted by X

label: text
content: ## Orientation of protein sequences: from N-terminus to C-terminus

label: text
content: A protein sequence always starts with an "M" (methionine; encoded by the start codon "AUG")

label: text
content: The stop codons ("UAA", "UAG" and "UGA") do not encode for any amino acid but terminate translation (sometimes they are represented as translating to "*", but the asterisk is not considered as part of the protein molecule)

content: ## Reverse strings, palindromes and rotations

label: text
content:
- The reverse of a string is a string with the same symbols but in reverse order

For example, if $s = "abc" (with a,b,c in$\Sigma $,$ \mathrm {a,b,c\in\mathbb{C}$

label: text
content: - A string that is the reverse of itself (e.g., $ s = "omordotuanuoraoarounautodromo") is called a palindrome

label: text
content: The empty string and all strings of length 1 are palindromes

label: text
content: Note: while some wordplays consider spaces as "moveable" because they aren't spoken, we consider as palindromes only strings where the order of all symbols (including spaces) is precisely reversed, e.g., we would consider stressed desserts to be a palindrome, but not a nut for a jar of tuna)

label: text
content: Difference for DNA/RNA: a palindromic DNA/RNA sequence is identical to its reverse complement (reading both strands 5' $\rightarrow3'$ )!$

label: text
content: Example: "GATC" is palindromic "CAAC" is not!

label: text
content: - A string $s = uv$ (with $u,v \in \Sigma^{*}$ is said to be a rotation of $t = vu$

label: text
content: As another example, the string "abc" has three different rotations:

label: text
content: ★ itself (with $u="abc", v=\varepsilon$

label: text
content: ★ bca (with $ u="bc" "bc", v="a") , and

label: text
content: ★ cab (with $u="c$ "c $" c$ v="ab"$

label: text
content: The number of possible rotations of a string is equal to its length!

label: text
content: ## Comparison of biological sequences

label: text
content: - An important goal is to define suitable methods for the comparison of sequences:

label: text
content: To assess or quantify "how different" or "how different" or "how similar" two or more sequences are

label: text
content: To identify similar sequences (with similar functions?) in databases

label: text
content: To identify the genomic locations of NGS reads

label: text
content: - We need to define suitable measures of distance or similarity, as well as efficient algorithms to compute them

label: text
content: - The measures should reflect as much as possible the different ways in which the sequences can be similar or different, and the processes or factors underlying the similarities and differences, for example:

label: text
content: Evolution of the sequences: what does it mean that we "share 50% of our genes with bananas"? More here:

label: text
content: https://medium.com/emergent-phenomenawe-share-50-of-genes-with-bananas-and 501-parent-is-one-of-ourparents-a-banana-495580649580458640586495801

label: text
content: Errors in data production (e.g., sequencing errors)

label: text
content: - Errors made my the cells, e.g., during DNA replication; more here: https://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/dna-replication-and-causes-of-mutation-409/

label: text
content: ## Technical errors in biological sequences

label: text
content: - Sequencing error: the sequencing machine identifies a wrong base/nucleotide in a sequence (e.g., "ACGCGGTGAACGTTGAAC" instead of "ACGCGTTTGAAC"

label: text
content: - Error rates change according to the sequencing platform: for Illumina sequencers (most widely used) <0.1%

label: text
content: That is, less than one sequencing error every 10000 base pairs

label: text
content: But: in 100 million reads of 200 bp length each you would still find up to 20 million sequencing errors ...

label: text
content: - Such errors cannot be ignored by algorithms employed in the analysis of the data

label: text
content: ## Biological errors in biological sequences

label: text
content: - Living cells replicate their DNA and replication errors are naturally part of this process

label: text
content: - Although cells possess very efficient (and beautiful!) error-correcting mechanisms acting at different points of DNA replication, some errors escape ("mutations") and are inherited by daughter cells

label: text
content: The "error rate" changes according to the organism and the different parts of the genome, roughly ranging from one every 100 million base pairs to (in some cases) one every thousands of base pairs

label: text
content: - What types of error does the cell make in replicating its DNA?

label: text
content: ## Biological errors in biological sequences

label: text
content: - Base substitutions ("single nucleotide polymorphisms/variants"; SNPs, SNVs)

label: text
content: Like for sequencing errors, the original base pair is erroneously replaced by another one. Depending on which base is altered/mutated, this may lead to disease

label: text
content: - Difference to sequencing errors: the latter affects only one read; mutations affect many (or all) reads which cover the mutated genomic location

label: text
content: - Insertions/deletions of small DNA fragments ("indels") (even of a single base pair)

label: text
content: ## Biological errors in biological sequences

label: text
content: ## Structural variants

label: text
content: Involve regions of DNA of about 1 kb and larger in size

label: text
content: Mentioned here for completeness (less important for the algorithms we discuss in this course)

label: text
content: Inversion of a genomic region (orientation inverted)

label: text
content: Translocation of a genomic region

label: text
content: ★ "inter-chromosomal": from one chromosome to another

label: text
content: ★ "intra-chromosomal": within a chromosome

label: text
content: - (Large-scale) insertions/deletions (as opposed to indels)

label: text
content: Duplications

label: text
content: ★ "tandem duplication": adjacent to original sequence

label: text
content: ★ or region duplicated elsewhere

label: text
content: ## Comparing strings: the edit distance

label: text
content: - The edit distance is a way of quantifying how dissimilar two strings (also of different length) are to one another by counting the minimum number of operations required to transform one string into the other

label: text
content: - Different definitions of an edit distance use different sets of string operations. In the Levenshtein distance the allowed operations are

label: text
content: removal

label: text
content: insertion

label: text
content: substitution

label: text
content: of a character in the string. Being the most common metric, the term "Levenshtein distance is often used interchangeably with edit distance as we will also do in this course)

label: text
content: - The edit distance was invented before bioinformatics but captures nicely "biological errors" in sequences

label: text
content: substition, insertion or deletion of a nucleotide

label: text
content: - Interesting also for other purposes, e.g., for spelling correction:

label: text
content: A user erroneously typed "graffe"; what did the user most likely mean? "graff" or "giraffe"?

content: ## Measuring sequence similarity

label: text
content: Better: "longest common subsequence"

label: text
content: - Subsequence: derived by deleting some, all or no characters; the order of the remaining elements remains unchanged

label: text
content: The remaining symbols need not be consecutive, e.g., "SUDAY" is a valid subsequence of "SATURDAY"

label: text
content: For each string a, both a itself and the empty string $\varepsilon$ are valid subsequences

label: text
content: Longest common subsequence (LCS) problem

label: text
content: - Note the difference between subsequence and substring (not: longest common substring problem)!

label: text
content: Substrings are consecutive letters from the original string

label: text
content: A string a of length n = |a| has 1 + $\sum_{i=1^{n} i = 1 + \frac{n+1$ substrings

label: text
content: How about the number of subsequences?

label: text
content: - Idea: a subsequence of $a$ can be described by a binary string $B$ of $n$ elements, telling us for each position $i$ if the corresponding character of $a$ is kept in the subsequence (1) or deleted (0). Example: $a=apple, B=1110111010 \rightarrow$

label: text
content: > Thus, the maximum number of possible subsequences of length n is the same as the number of binary strings of that length: $ 2^{n}

label: text
content: ## The LCS algorithm

label: text
content: - Let a and b be two strings with $|a| = n$ and $|b|=m$

label: text
content: Let a(i) and b(j) be prefixes of length 0 $\leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq m$

label: text
content: - Let $L C S ( a, b )$ be the length of the longest common subsequence

label: text
content: Of course, we have $L C S ( a,\varepsilon)=0$

label: text
content: - We can compute $L C S ( a, b )$ using

label: formula

label: text
content: Maximum instead of minimum!

label: text
content: - Increase the score by 1 for $a_{i}=b_{j}$, no increase for all edit operations (insertion, deletion, change of symbol)

label: text
content: > Thus, LCS will be the maximum number of matching symbols without changing the order (minimum number of gaps and mismatches)

label: text
content: As for the edit distance, we can use pointers to keep track of the choices

content: ## Combining distance and similarity

label: text
content: - We have seen two symmetrical approaches for comparing sequences/strings

label: text
content: Edit distance measures the number of differences between two strings, where the edit operations used reproduce what makes sequences different (e.g., difference in nucleotide sequences due to evolution)

label: text
content: > Longest common subsequence: measures the number of characters in the strings which have been "conserved", that is, unchanged from an evolutionary point of view

label: text
content:
- Idea: combine the two approaches into a single one!

Define a similarity measure for two strings a and b such that

label: text
content: > "differences" have a negative effect: negative weight for gap (insertion, deletion) and mismatch (substitution); often called "penalty"

label: text
content: > "conserved letters" have a positive effect: positive weight for match

label: text
content: ## A note on gap penalties

label: text
content: - There are actually different models of gap penalties:

label: text
content: > Linear gap penalty: gap penalty: gap penalty for a single symbol is multiplied by the total length of a gap (this is what we implicitly used so far), e.g., "---" counts the same as 3 $\times$ - $^ {3}$ \times $-$ - $

label: text
content: - Constant gap penalty: fixed negative score for the entire gap, regardless of its length also when the gap covers multiple symbols of the other sequence) e.g. "- -" counts the same as an individual "- " -"

label: text
content: ★ Used if fewer, larger, gaps are preferred, thus leaving larger contiguous sections

label: text
content: - Affine gap penalty (most widely used): combines the constant and linear gap penalty by defining:

label: text
content: 1 Constant gap opening penalty: penalty for opening a gap (first “-”

label: text
content: 2 Linear gap extension penalty: penalty for extending the length of an existing gap by 1 " -"

label: text
content: ★ Usually: gap opening penalty > gap extension penalty; i.e., it's easier to extend an existing gap then to open a new one

label: text
content: ★ Purpose: prefer not to have gaps, but if they are necessary prefer fewer large ones
